question_text: Many wine regions can produce wines at a wide range of price points. Referencing at least two of such regions, compare and contrast methods of managing vineyards for high priced wines and low priced wines.
command_word_demand: Comparing and contrasting meant analysing the relative value of the approaches from the high-price vs low-price perspective, not describing practices: "A number of responses simply described viticultural practices without actually doing the analyses the question requires."

required_elements.element: A relatively detailed treatment of at least two regions, not a survey of many
required_elements.quote: The question required a relatively detailed look at least two regions; some papers provided a scatter- shot of many regions' approaches, but did not address the relative value of these approaches from the question's perspective of addressing high and low value wine production.

required_elements.element: Address between five and seven distinct issues of vineyard management, rather than over-developing a few
required_elements.quote: While the question allowed for many issues to be compared and contrasted, the Examiners felt that there were between five and seven that specifically needed to be addressed.

required_elements.element: Yield vs. quality and price as one of the compared issues
required_elements.quote: It was frustrating, as one Examiner noted, to see much written well about yield vs. quality and price, but then nothing on the implications of harvesting for high vs. low priced wines.

required_elements.element: The implications of harvesting (hand vs machine, timing, selection) for high vs low priced wines
required_elements.quote: It was frustrating, as one Examiner noted, to see much written well about yield vs. quality and price, but then nothing on the implications of harvesting for high vs. low priced wines.

required_elements.element: Examine the financial implications and costs of the vineyard decisions taken, with facts and figures
required_elements.quote: there is a lack of in-depth knowledge, facts and figures relating to the costs of viticulture and wine.

credit_signals.signal: Clear organisation with an explicit region-by-region comparison and analysis at estate as well as regional level
credit_signals.quote: Passing papers were well organised, with clearly defined comparison of the regions and with good analyses comparing methods used by different estates and different regions.

credit_signals.signal: Going beyond viticultural description to the financial consequences of each decision — even passing papers were weak here
credit_signals.quote: Even here, however, it was often noted that many papers failed to more closely examine the financial implications of some decisions taken.

penalty_signals.signal: Describing viticultural practices instead of analysing them against the price-point question
penalty_signals.quote: A number of responses simply described viticultural practices without actually doing the analyses the question requires.

penalty_signals.signal: Scatter-shot coverage of many regions without addressing the relative value of their approaches
penalty_signals.quote: some papers provided a scatter- shot of many regions' approaches, but did not address the relative value of these approaches from the question's perspective of addressing high and low value wine production.

penalty_signals.signal: Understanding present but examples absent or generic
penalty_signals.quote: In other instances, there was clear understanding, but virtually no examples to make the discussion complete, or with generic ones at best.

penalty_signals.signal: Over-developing some issues at the cost of omitting a key one — a near-miss failure mode
penalty_signals.quote: Too many papers, sadly, were 'close' but missed because of omitting a key issue at the expense of too much discussion about some of the others.

examples_expected.specificity: Named regions treated in detail (at least two) plus named estates within them; generic examples were explicitly marked down
examples_expected.quote: In other instances, there was clear understanding, but virtually no examples to make the discussion complete, or with generic ones at best.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as a broad tour of global viticulture rather than a detailed comparison anchored in at least two regions
scope_traps.quote: The question required a relatively detailed look at least two regions; some papers provided a scatter- shot of many regions' approaches…

performance_note: "Unfortunately, this was the least well answered question on Paper 1." Passing papers were well organised with clearly defined regional comparison, but even they under-examined financial implications.
extraction_notes: The examiners state that "between five and seven" issues specifically needed addressing but never enumerate the full list — only yield vs. quality/price and harvesting implications are named. A grader cannot check the remaining three-to-five against the report, so the five-to-seven requirement should be applied as a breadth expectation, not an itemised checklist. Also note: the paper_preamble for 2018 Paper 1 is mis-segmented in report_segments.json — it opens with the PRACTICAL exam papers' commentary (Chardonnay, Kumeu River, Brunello etc.) and only reaches the actual Theory Paper 1 General Comments at the very end. Nothing was extracted from the practical portion.

question_text: Identify the most important trunk diseases in vineyards around the world. How can they be best controlled and managed?
command_word: identify … how can they be best controlled and managed
command_word_demand: A two-part question where both parts had to be answered in depth: "Critical to success here was answering both parts of this question. Less successful papers did well on identifying the most important trunk diseases, but failed to consider in depth control and management."

required_elements.element: Answer both parts — identification AND control/management
required_elements.quote: Critical to success here was answering both parts of this question.

required_elements.element: Cover at least three of the four to five key global trunk diseases — not just Esca and Eutypa
required_elements.quote: A passing paper had to include at least three of the four to five key diseases noted globally. Many papers discussed Esca and Eutypa, but left out Botryosphaeria and Phomopsis.

required_elements.element: Acknowledge the global reach of these diseases — regional differences, varietal susceptibility, differing treatments
required_elements.quote: Key to a successful answer was an acknowledgement of the global reach of these diseases: differences, varieties, treatments.

required_elements.element: Compare and contrast control techniques according to location and climate
required_elements.quote: Examiners commented that many papers simply didn't do an adequate job of comparing and contrasting various techniques to deal with these diseases depending on location and climate.

required_elements.element: Highlight diseases that specifically affect younger vines, such as Petri disease or black foot
required_elements.quote: The best papers highlighted diseases affecting younger vines specifically, like Petri disease or black foot disease.

credit_signals.signal: Clear essay architecture plus critical analysis with globally-ranged comparative examples
credit_signals.quote: Answers the question and answers key points. Good introduction, conclusion and structure. Includes good critical analysis with good comparative examples to support analysis, with a global range. Good writing style- A+

credit_signals.signal: Coverage of young-vine trunk diseases beyond the standard Esca/Eutypa pair
credit_signals.quote: The best papers highlighted diseases affecting younger vines specifically, like Petri disease or black foot disease.

penalty_signals.signal: Identifying diseases well but treating control and management superficially
penalty_signals.quote: Less successful papers did well on identifying the most important trunk diseases, but failed to consider in depth control and management.

penalty_signals.signal: Factual errors about vine age or disease aetiology
penalty_signals.quote: Factual errors, such as claiming that five to seven year old vines are middle-aged, or that GTD's are caused by viruses, not fungi, reflected poorly on candidates' knowledge and weakened their argument significantly.

penalty_signals.signal: Relying on one or two examples traceable to a single textbook or article
penalty_signals.quote: Examiners noted a strong dependence on one or two particular examples that are indicative of the same 'textbook' source, or an article.

examples_expected.specificity: Comparative examples with genuine global range; drawing all examples from a single textbook source was criticised
examples_expected.quote: Includes good critical analysis with good comparative examples to support analysis, with a global range.

scope_traps.trap: Writing at length about phylloxera or flavescence dorée, which are not trunk diseases
scope_traps.quote: A few papers got into long discussions about phylloxera and/or flavescence dorée; these are not trunk diseases!

performance_note: "This technically demanding question was answered relatively well, given the precise knowledge required."
extraction_notes: named_in_report here lists the trunk diseases the report itself names (four expected, plus two young-vine diseases praised in the best papers), not geographic examples — the commentary names no regions. The report says 'four to five key diseases noted globally' but names only four (Esca, Eutypa, Botryosphaeria, Phomopsis), so the identity of a possible fifth is not recoverable from the report.

question_text: Is the use of cover crops worthwhile in viticulture?
command_word_demand: An opinion question requiring a judgement of effectiveness, evidenced: "Perhaps because the question had a certain "Op-Ed" aspect, requiring a candidate to express an opinion (based upon sound factual examples and knowledge, however), this made for more fluid discussion." The analysis had to place cover crops in a wider viticultural context and judge them: "The question as set was asking for an analysis that looked at cover crops as one component of viticulture, perhaps in relation to climate change, or to the unique challenge of a particular terroir, but also considered the effectiveness of a given approach."

required_elements.element: Demonstrate what cover crops actually do, differentiated by climate and by water availability
required_elements.quote: This question demanded clear understanding of what cover crops do, in different climates, and depending on availability of water.

required_elements.element: Judge utility against intended purpose rather than listing where cover crops are or are not used
required_elements.quote: It was not enough to list examples of where cover crops are used or not; it was necessary to discuss their utility … in the context of their intended purpose.

required_elements.element: Address both advantages and disadvantages, with examples showing where they are 'worthwhile'
required_elements.quote: Advantages and disadvantages needed to be addressed, and examples used to demonstrate where the use of cover crops may be considered 'worthwhile'.

required_elements.element: Develop four to six positive or negative reasons, each properly discussed
required_elements.quote: Good candidates used four to six positive or negative reasons, each discussed well.

required_elements.element: Site-specific nuance — slope, site vigour, frost potential, organic certification
required_elements.quote: Good answers were attuned to the particular uniqueness of various sites relative to slope, site vigor and frost potential or certification for organic viticulture.

required_elements.element: Economic utility — the extra cost of planting and cultivating cover crops relative to wine type and value
required_elements.quote: It was also useful to consider the economic utility of cover crops, considering the extra cost entailed in planting/cultivating cover crops relative to the wine type and value produced.

credit_signals.signal: Nuanced, site-specific utility arguments — e.g. erosion control and water penetration in the Douro
credit_signals.quote: Good papers noted more nuanced utility; for example, cover crops used to prevent erosion and help with water penetration in the harsh Douro climate.

credit_signals.signal: Framing cover crops as one component of a viticultural system, e.g. against climate change or a particular terroir challenge
credit_signals.quote: The question as set was asking for an analysis that looked at cover crops as one component of viticulture, perhaps in relation to climate change, or to the unique challenge of a particular terroir, but also considered the effectiveness of a given approach.

penalty_signals.signal: Sweeping unqualified generalisations in place of evidenced opinion
penalty_signals.quote: In a few papers, however this led to sweeping generalizations, such as "Cover crops are very necessary for viticulture".

penalty_signals.signal: Descriptive answers, however well exampled, that answer 'what do cover crops do?' rather than 'are they worthwhile?'
penalty_signals.quote: A number of papers, Examiners noted, were overly descriptive, though studded with examples. These generally answered a different question than posed, i.e. What do cover crops do?

penalty_signals.signal: Narrow argument resting on only one or two reasons
penalty_signals.quote: Those that did not focused narrowly on fewer ones such as soaking up excess rainfall in cooler humid areas, or not using them in more arid climates.

examples_expected.specificity: Site-specific examples tied to a stated purpose (slope, vigour, frost, erosion, certification) — a list of places using cover crops was explicitly insufficient
examples_expected.quote: It was not enough to list examples of where cover crops are used or not; it was necessary to discuss their utility … in the context of their intended purpose.

scope_traps.trap: Answering the descriptive question 'What do cover crops do?' instead of the evaluative one set
scope_traps.quote: These generally answered a different question than posed, i.e. What do cover crops do?

performance_note: "This was the most successfully answered question on this year's Paper 1."
extraction_notes: A page number ('11') intruded into the PDF text mid-sentence in the 'utility in the context of their intended purpose' quote and has been trimmed with an ellipsis; the original reads 'their utility 11 in the context'.

question_text: What is the role of pruning when managing an established vineyard?
command_word_demand: The question asked for the FUNCTION of pruning, not its techniques: "The question was about how pruning a vine affects vineyard growth, quality and economic value and not about describing pruning techniques."

definitions_required.term: pruning (in the context of an established, functioning vineyard)
definitions_required.quote: This was a question that needed a definition of pruning, relative to working in a functioning vineyard.

required_elements.element: Define and explain the key purposes of pruning, kept in the context of the question
required_elements.quote: A good answer had to define and explain the key purposes of pruning, but always in the context of the question.

required_elements.element: Establishing yield as the primary purpose, with method varying by wine style
required_elements.quote: A passing paper had to deal with the primary purpose of pruning, establishing yield, with comparison and methodology depending on wine style; e.g. short cane pruning with densely planted Pinot noir in Gevrey Chambertin vs. high-trained quadrilateral cordon with low density spacing in the Central Valley of California.

required_elements.element: Pruning relative to specific grape varieties and wine styles
required_elements.quote: It was critical for a passing paper to address the issue of pruning relative to specific varieties and wine styles, and the timing of pruning and treatments for pruning wounds (at least in passing).

required_elements.element: Timing of pruning and treatment of pruning wounds — at least in passing
required_elements.quote: It was critical for a passing paper to address the issue of pruning relative to specific varieties and wine styles, and the timing of pruning and treatments for pruning wounds (at least in passing).

required_elements.element: How WINTER pruning affects ventilation, ease of harvest, disease control and frost alleviation as well as yield
required_elements.quote: It was clear to Examiners that too many answers lacked understanding of how winter pruning can strongly affect aspects of ventilation, ease of harvest, disease control or frost alleviation as well as yield.

required_elements.element: Cover the full pruning calendar — winter, spring/summer (hedging, sucker thinning) and green pruning of clusters
required_elements.quote: Smart answers addressed winter pruning, spring/summer pruning (hedging, sucker thinning), and where appropriate, 'green' pruning of less mature clusters to even out maturation or remove deficient fruit (under-ripe, raisined, or rotten berries).

required_elements.element: Advantages and disadvantages of hand vs mechanical pruning, especially economic cost and wine style
required_elements.quote: Good papers addressed both the advantages and disadvantages of hand-pruning vs. mechanical, especially with regard to the economic costs and style of wine being produced.

credit_signals.signal: Concrete paired contrasts of pruning regime against density and wine style
credit_signals.quote: e.g. short cane pruning with densely planted Pinot noir in Gevrey Chambertin vs. high-trained quadrilateral cordon with low density spacing in the Central Valley of California.

credit_signals.signal: Linking pruning to economic value, not only to growth and quality
credit_signals.quote: The question was about how pruning a vine affects vineyard growth, quality and economic value and not about describing pruning techniques.

penalty_signals.signal: Writing about the mechanics of pruning rather than the role it plays
penalty_signals.quote: Too many non-passing papers were "more concerned with the mechanics of pruning than the role it plays", as one Examiner commented.

penalty_signals.signal: Treating the winter-pruning benefits only through summer pruning or general canopy management
penalty_signals.quote: More answers addressed these issues from the perspective of summer pruning and/or simple canopy management.

penalty_signals.signal: Generic arguments and generic examples that fail to demonstrate real understanding
penalty_signals.quote: Again, this question saw several papers that used generic arguments or examples, without showing more concrete ones that illustrated the writer's real understanding and consideration of the question.

examples_expected.specificity: Concrete variety + place + training/pruning-system combinations (e.g. cane-pruned Pinot Noir in Gevrey Chambertin vs quadrilateral cordon in California's Central Valley); generic examples were criticised
examples_expected.quote: Again, this question saw several papers that used generic arguments or examples, without showing more concrete ones that illustrated the writer's real understanding and consideration of the question.

scope_traps.trap: Reading the question as 'describe pruning techniques' rather than 'what does pruning achieve'
scope_traps.quote: The question was about how pruning a vine affects vineyard growth, quality and economic value and not about describing pruning techniques.

performance_note: No attempt or pass rate is given. "Too many non-passing papers were "more concerned with the mechanics of pruning than the role it plays", as one Examiner commented."

question_text: Old vines have a mystique to them. What are the practical challenges and solutions to maintaining vineyards of old vines?
command_word: what are the practical challenges and solutions
command_word_demand: The question was about the viticultural difficulty of keeping old vineyards alive, not about the merits of old-vine wine: "But this question was all about the unique viticultural challenges old vines present in order to continue their existence." Both halves — challenges AND maintenance solutions — were required: "The issue of 'maintenance' had to be addressed."

definitions_required.quote: It was important to define old vines; Examiners saw everything from 15 to 20 years old as a minimum age, to 60 years. Considering that the average lifespan today globally for vines is in the 20 to 30 year range, a passing paper had to consider old vines in the context of the location being … discussed, and be clear about how this definition is often conditioned by regulations (e.g. the Barossa Charter), the historical nature of a vineyard region, or its modernity.

required_elements.element: Define old vines in the context of the location discussed, referencing regulation, regional history or modernity — any defensible definition was accepted if the examples matched it
required_elements.quote: Provided examples were given which accorded with the writer's premise, different definitions for old vines were allowed.

required_elements.element: The problems confronting older vines: poor vigour, declining productivity, disease susceptibility (especially trunk diseases and pruning wounds)
required_elements.quote: This question required a substantial knowledge about what problems confront older vines; whether these are related to poor vigour, decrease in productivity, susceptibility to disease, especially trunk diseases or pruning wounds.

required_elements.element: Explicitly address 'maintenance' — the solutions half of the question
required_elements.quote: The issue of 'maintenance' had to be addressed.

required_elements.element: The economics of maintaining an old vineyard: rising mechanisation and lower costs elsewhere vs the expensive manual labour old vines demand
required_elements.quote: The economics of maintaining an old vineyard had also to be considered, particularly in light of increasing mechanization in vineyards with lower costs, vs. the expensive manual labour that old vines almost always require.

required_elements.element: The difficulty or impossibility of mechanising the care of old vineyards
required_elements.quote: A key challenge for maintaining old vineyards is the difficulty/inability to use more mechanization for their care. This was certainly something that a passing paper had to address; a number of papers did not do so, or only with a minor reference.

required_elements.element: Weigh over-fertilisation of old vines against soil or rootstock vigour
required_elements.quote: Over-fertilization of old vines, in the hope of keeping them healthier, had to be weighed in relation to soil or rootstock vigour, as this can stress and overtax an old vine's system.

credit_signals.signal: Depth over breadth — fewer issues, thoroughly argued, scored higher than a catalogue
credit_signals.quote: Answers that focussed on fewer issues relative to the question, but did so thoroughly, generally achieved higher marks than those which tried to throw in as much as possible, without the appropriate depth of knowledge or examples to support the argument.

credit_signals.signal: Anchoring the old-vine definition to a codified regional standard
credit_signals.quote: be clear about how this definition is often conditioned by regulations (e.g. the Barossa Charter), the historical nature of a vineyard region, or its modernity.

penalty_signals.signal: Arguing the subjective superiority of old-vine wine instead of examining the practical challenges — an outright fail
penalty_signals.quote: Not addressing these issues and focussing mainly on the potentially higher quality from a subjective belief in old vines making the best wines, without the critical examination dictated by the question, resulted in failure.

penalty_signals.signal: Factual error: claiming old vines are MORE susceptible to drought or water stress
penalty_signals.quote: Several papers made the mistake of saying that old vines are more susceptible to drought/water stress. As the Examiners noted repeatedly the opposite is true, as evidenced by their longevity under diverse, often harsh conditions, in places like South Africa, Australia, Santorini and elsewhere.

penalty_signals.signal: Omitting or barely mentioning the mechanisation problem
penalty_signals.quote: This was certainly something that a passing paper had to address; a number of papers did not do so, or only with a minor reference.

penalty_signals.signal: Breadth without the depth of knowledge or examples to support it
penalty_signals.quote: those which tried to throw in as much as possible, without the appropriate depth of knowledge or examples to support the argument.

examples_expected.specificity: Examples must be consistent with the candidate's own stated definition of 'old vines'; old-vine regions cited by the report are South Africa, Australia and Santorini, and the Barossa Charter as a regulatory definition
examples_expected.quote: Provided examples were given which accorded with the writer's premise, different definitions for old vines were allowed.

scope_traps.trap: Taking the 'mystique' framing as an invitation to argue that old-vine wines are superior
scope_traps.quote: The topic of this question is one which fascinates anyone interested in wine, everyone has an opinion about the superiority of old vine wine! But this question was all about the unique viticultural challenges old vines present in order to continue their existence.

performance_note: No attempt or pass rate is given. Failure is explicitly attributed to writing about old-vine quality rather than practical challenges, and to omitting the mechanisation issue.
extraction_notes: A page number ('12') intruded into the PDF text mid-sentence in the definition quote and has been trimmed with an ellipsis; the original reads 'in the context of the location being 12 discussed'. Note the report asserts a factual position — that old vines are LESS susceptible to drought stress — which a grader should apply as an examiner expectation.

question_text: Examine the advantages and disadvantages of deliberate stem inclusion, or additions, during the winemaking process.
command_word_demand: Both sides had to be argued, across the whole process: "Students needed to demonstrate an understanding of why and how stems are used in the winemaking process and then discuss the advantages and disadvantages of their inclusion." The Paper 2 General Comments reinforce this: "If the words 'advantages and disadvantages' are in the question they need to be addressed and discussed."

required_elements.element: Cover the entire winemaking process, not just fermentation
required_elements.quote: We expected candidates to cover the entire winemaking process, within the scope of Paper 2, not just fermentation.

required_elements.element: Cover white, rosé and red table wine, with sparkling and fortified at least mentioned
required_elements.quote: We also expected students to cover white, rosé and red table winemaking as well as mentioning sparkling and fortified wines.

required_elements.element: Explain WHY and HOW stems are used before evaluating them
required_elements.quote: Students needed to demonstrate an understanding of why and how stems are used in the winemaking process and then discuss the advantages and disadvantages of their inclusion.

required_elements.element: Argue the case AGAINST stem inclusion, given that most wine is destemmed
required_elements.quote: Whilst the argument for stems was often good, the argument against the use of stems was often lacking. Given most wines are destemmed, this could have been argued better.

required_elements.element: Locate stem inclusion in the process — where it may be warranted and what the outcome is, both good and bad
required_elements.quote: Candidates are reminded to think about winemaking as a process and to consider where stem inclusion may be warranted and what the outcome of that would be - both advantageous and disadvantageous.

required_elements.element: Varietal contrast: stems favour Grenache, Syrah and Pinot Noir; cite varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot as less appropriate
required_elements.quote: Advantages for stems tend to be concentrated in the three varieties: Grenache, Syrah and Pinot Noir. Given comparisons were needed, varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot could have been cited as varieties that may be less appropriate for stem inclusion.

required_elements.element: Discuss stems in white wine, including natural and qvevri styles
required_elements.quote: Students tended to disregard stems within white wines with alarming regularity. Given the amount of natural wines, qvevri style wines, etc, more could have been discussed.

credit_signals.signal: Staying with the question across all styles and the whole process rather than surveying practice
credit_signals.quote: Candidates who did well focussed on the question at hand - the advantages and disadvantages of deliberate stem inclusion across all wine styles and the whole winemaking process.

penalty_signals.signal: A list of who uses stems, with examples standing in for the argument
penalty_signals.quote: Too many candidates just gave us a list of who is doing what with stems. Examples should be used to support an argument, not be the argument themselves.

penalty_signals.signal: Ignoring stems in white wine
penalty_signals.quote: Students tended to disregard stems within white wines with alarming regularity.

penalty_signals.signal: Leaning on the same widely-circulated seminar reference as everyone else
penalty_signals.quote: On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac.

penalty_signals.signal: Over-familiar tone when citing producers by first name
penalty_signals.quote: when using examples over-familiarity, even if those individuals being cited are well-known to the candidate, does not strike a suitable tone: "At Churton in Marlborough, Sam will decide to include stems…"

examples_expected.specificity: Examples must support the argument, not constitute it; the report warns against the mass-cited seminar reference and against over-familiar naming of producers
examples_expected.quote: Examples should be used to support an argument, not be the argument themselves.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as red-wine (and fermentation-stage) only

examples_expected.specificity: Examples are optional support for a statement, not a requirement of the format
